prose-img:max-h-[13.75rem] md:prose-img:max-h-[27.5rem] xl:prose-img:max-h-[30rem] prose-img:!mx-0 [&amp;_th]:text-[18px]"><p><em>The platform that makes every business feel human.</em></p>
<p><a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=818wTRa1e48" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" node="[object Object]">Watch the Series B announcement video</a></p>
<p>By the time you die, you will have spent 43 days of your life on hold.</p>
<p>Forty-three days of “<em>your call is important to us</em>.” Forty-three days of menu trees and transfer hand-offs and re-entering your account number into the keypad and re-explaining yourself to a fourth person. Multiply that across the country, and Americans spend 900 million hours a year on hold. Multiply it across the world, and you get to <strong>three trillion minutes a year</strong> of business-to-customer phone calls. This is the channel that companies continue to pay billions of dollars to build, staff, maintain, and apologize for.</p>
<p>We started Vapi to end it.</p>
<p>Today we&#x27;re announcing our $50M Series B, led by Peak XV, with participation from YC, M12 (Microsoft&#x27;s Venture Fund), Kleiner Perkins, and our earlier investors. It brings our total funding to $72M. The round closed on the back of a year in which our enterprise revenue grew 10x, and our agents crossed <strong>1,000,000,000 calls</strong> handled. But this post isn&#x27;t about the round. It&#x27;s about the bet behind it.</p>
<h2><strong>The spark</strong></h2>
<p>In the summer of 2023, I was depressed and obsessed with a problem.</p>
<p>I&#x27;d been working with speech models for years and could see three curves bending at the same time: latency dropping, models getting smarter, cost falling, all at once, across the entire voice stack. Stitch them together carefully, and you could build something that felt like a person on the other end of the line.</p>
<p>So for my daily walks, I built an AI therapist named Harmon. I printed business cards. I rode the bus around SF and handed them out to strangers. <em>Call this number. Get free therapy.</em></p>
<p>Nobody wanted AI therapy. But the first time I had a real, fluid, back-and-forth conversation with a model on the phone, I knew. Not in the abstract, in my gut. This is how everything is going to work. Voice is the default way humans have always connected. We were about to start talking to technology, and our technology was going to talk back.</p>
<h2><strong>The gap</strong></h2>
<p>It’s two years later, and that moment is about to land in everyone&#x27;s pocket. Think of where Siri, ChatGPT voice, and Gemini Live are heading: an assistant that listens, remembers, and talks back like a friend. That&#x27;s the device every consumer will have within eighteen months - voice-native, context-aware, with you all day. People will talk to their software more than they tap on it. The bar for what a conversation can feel like is about to reset, and it will reset fast.</p>
<p>With all this technology readily available, why should those same people call their insurance company and get an IVR from 1998?</p>
<p>That gap - between the conversation a consumer has at home and the one an enterprise serves them on a customer service line - is about to become the most embarrassing thing about every Fortune 500 company in the world. Customers will start punishing it. Brands will start losing because of it.</p>
<p>We are building the platform that closes the gap. One that makes every business feel human.</p>
<h2><strong>The bet</strong></h2>
<p>Most of the voice AI market right now is selling cost reduction. <em>Replace the human, save the money, and get more profitable.</em> That&#x27;s a fine starting wedge, but it’s not the end game.</p>
<p>The end game is taking the call center - the largest cost center in most enterprises - and turning it into a revenue center. A place customers actually like to call into.</p>
<p>Think about that for a second. The contact center at AT&amp;T, JP Morgan, State Farm - historically a budget line measured in billions, optimized to be <em>as cheap as possible to make the angry customer go away</em>. Now, picture an agent that doesn&#x27;t just resolve the call but resolves it better than any human ever has. Closes more. Retain more. Sells more. Listens better. Knows more about your customer. Every attribute of your best human agents is scaled to your entire customer base</p>
<p>That requires voice agents that get measurably better with every call. A platform where every conversation is a training signal, every resolution is a labeled example, and every miss becomes the next iteration&#x27;s learning. The agent your customers talk to next month will be obviously better than the one they talked to today.</p>
<p>Self-improving voice agents, at production scale, with a feedback loop tight enough that the line between <em>AI</em> and <em>the best person you have ever talked to</em> stops being just an idea.</p>
<p>That&#x27;s what we&#x27;re building.</p>
<h2><strong>The unglamorous half</strong></h2>
<p>You can&#x27;t put agents like these in front of millions of customers without the boring half of the work: compliance, observability, hard guardrails, predictable latency under load, and clean escalation to humans when the situation calls for one. Every call is a production workload. Every call has the potential to embarrass the company on the other end of it, if things do go wrong.</p>
<p>We&#x27;ve spent years on this part. It&#x27;s why Amazon Ring went from evaluation to running 100% of inbound on Vapi in two weeks. It&#x27;s why we win in financial services, healthcare, and insurance - categories where one bad call can cost more than a year of savings and reputational damage.</p>
<p>Governance and outperformance are not separable. Without governance, no enterprise should put an agent live. Without agents that outperform humans, governance is just paperwork. We have built a foundation and are continuing to invest in both at the same time. That&#x27;s what a platform is.</p>
<h2><strong>What it looks like when it works</strong></h2>
<p><strong>Amazon Ring</strong> evaluated dozens of vendors but decided on Vapi and went to production in two weeks. Today, every inbound call to one of the most demanding consumer support operations in the world runs through Vapi. Even more impressive, CSAT went up. Jason Mitura, VP of Software Development, said it simply: “A lot of AI tools promise great outcomes. Vapi has delivered on them.”</p>
<p><strong>Kavak</strong>, the largest used-car marketplace in Latin America, made a company-wide bet on agents. Their CPO, Alejandro, went to the CEO and pitched a rebuild of every workflow - sales, operations, support - around voice AI, with the entire company either building or tuning agents. They started with one use case. They now run dozens. They built memory and personalization on top of our platform themselves, so a returning customer picks up exactly where they left off. We didn&#x27;t ship that. They did; that is the power of our platform. Their call center became a revenue center. They doubled revenue in their Mexico market.</p>
<p><strong>Instawork</strong> moved candidate interviews from humans to agents. Supply doubled. The agent never has a bad day, so every candidate gets the same clean interview, whether at 2 pm or 2 am. Some candidates stay on for thirty minutes just to talk about their lives.</p>
<p>A million developers have built on Vapi. Millions of agents have been created. We&#x27;ve handled more than a billion calls. We did almost no marketing to get there. The product is just that good, and the word spread.</p>
<p>In every one of these cases, the same thing happens: customers stop noticing. The business, on the other end of the line, starts to feel like a human.</p>
<h2><strong>What this round funds</strong></h2>
<p>With this round, we are focusing our investment in three places. <strong>Distribution</strong>, so the enterprises that should be evaluating us are evaluating us. <strong>Delivery</strong>, so customers go from &quot;we want to do this&quot; to &quot;we are doing this&quot; in weeks instead of quarters. And the engineering investment that matters most - <strong>core infrastructure, governance, and the self-improvement loop</strong> that turns every call into the agent&#x27;s next training signal.</p>
<p>We are continuing to focus on building the parts that actually let enterprises ship with confidence. With tools like Composer, Monitoring, and Simulations - launched over the past few months - customers can close the loop between building an agent, testing it against reality, and adapting it when reality pushes back. You can watch every call. You can catch the failure before your customer does.</p>
<p>The end state is a platform where the agent that picks up the phone tomorrow is reliably better than the one that picked up the phone today. We are building toward that, every day, at every layer.</p>
<h2><strong>The big claim</strong></h2>
<p>There is a generational company to be built in voice.</p>
<p>Three trillion minutes a year of business-to-customer voice. A category Twilio served for fifteen years and barely scratched. The biggest cost center in the Fortune 500, sitting there, waiting to become a revenue driver, and almost nobody is in the room.</p>
<p>But we are. We are building the platform that makes every business human.</p>
<p>If you want to spend the next few years on the most consequential thing you can do in AI right now, <a href="https://vapi.ai/careers" node="[object Object]">come build it with us</a>.</p>
<p>A billion calls in, and we’re just getting started.</p>

→\"]}]]}]]}]\n"])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"56:T22b6,"])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"*The platform that makes every business feel human.*\n\n[Watch the Series B announcement video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=818wTRa1e48)\n\nBy the time you die, you will have spent 43 days of your life on hold.\n\nForty-three days of “*your call is important to us*.” Forty-three days of menu trees and transfer hand-offs and re-entering your account number into the keypad and re-explaining yourself to a fourth person. Multiply that across the country, and Americans spend 900 million hours a year on hold. Multiply it across the world, and you get to **three trillion minutes a year** of business-to-customer phone calls. This is the channel that companies continue to pay billions of dollars to build, staff, maintain, and apologize for.\n\nWe started Vapi to end it.\n\nToday we're announcing our $50M Series B, led by Peak XV, with participation from YC, M12 (Microsoft's Venture Fund), Kleiner Perkins, and our earlier investors. It brings our total funding to $72M. The round closed on the back of a year in which our enterprise revenue grew 10x, and our agents crossed **1,000,000,000 calls** handled. But this post isn't about the round. It's about the bet behind it.\n\n## **The spark**\n\nIn the summer of 2023, I was depressed and obsessed with a problem.\n\nI'd been working with speech models for years and could see three curves bending at the same time: latency dropping, models getting smarter, cost falling, all at once, across the entire voice stack. Stitch them together carefully, and you could build something that felt like a person on the other end of the line.\n\nSo for my daily walks, I built an AI therapist named Harmon. I printed business cards. I rode the bus around SF and handed them out to strangers. *Call this number. Get free therapy.*\n\nNobody wanted AI therapy. But the first time I had a real, fluid, back-and-forth conversation with a model on the phone, I knew. Not in the abstract, in my gut. This is how everything is going to work. Voice is the default way humans have always connected. We were about to start talking to technology, and our technology was going to talk back.\n\n## **The gap**\n\nIt’s two years later, and that moment is about to land in everyone's pocket. Think of where Siri, ChatGPT voice, and Gemini Live are heading: an assistant that listens, remembers, and talks back like a friend. That's the device every consumer will have within eighteen months \\- voice-native, context-aware, with you all day. People will talk to their software more than they tap on it. The bar for what a conversation can feel like is about to reset, and it will reset fast.\n\nWith all this technology readily available, why should those same people call their insurance company and get an IVR from 1998?\n\nThat gap \\- between the conversation a consumer has at home and the one an enterprise serves them on a customer service line \\- is about to become the most embarrassing thing about every Fortune 500 company in the world. Customers will start punishing it. Brands will start losing because of it.\n\nWe are building the platform that closes the gap. One that makes every business feel human.\n\n## **The bet**\n\nMost of the voice AI market right now is selling cost reduction. *Replace the human, save the money, and get more profitable.* That's a fine starting wedge, but it’s not the end game.\n\nThe end game is taking the call center \\- the largest cost center in most enterprises \\- and turning it into a revenue center. A place customers actually like to call into.\n\nThink about that for a second. The contact center at AT\\\u0026T, JP Morgan, State Farm \\- historically a budget line measured in billions, optimized to be *as cheap as possible to make the angry customer go away*. Now, picture an agent that doesn't just resolve the call but resolves it better than any human ever has. Closes more. Retain more. Sells more. Listens better. Knows more about your customer. Every attribute of your best human agents is scaled to your entire customer base\n\nThat requires voice agents that get measurably better with every call. A platform where every conversation is a training signal, every resolution is a labeled example, and every miss becomes the next iteration's learning. The agent your customers talk to next month will be obviously better than the one they talked to today.\n\nSelf-improving voice agents, at production scale, with a feedback loop tight enough that the line between *AI* and *the best person you have ever talked to* stops being just an idea.\n\nThat's what we're building.\n\n## **The unglamorous half**\n\nYou can't put agents like these in front of millions of customers without the boring half of the work: compliance, observability, hard guardrails, predictable latency under load, and clean escalation to humans when the situation calls for one. Every call is a production workload. Every call has the potential to embarrass the company on the other end of it, if things do go wrong.\n\nWe've spent years on this part. It's why Amazon Ring went from evaluation to running 100% of inbound on Vapi in two weeks. It's why we win in financial services, healthcare, and insurance \\- categories where one bad call can cost more than a year of savings and reputational damage.\n\nGovernance and outperformance are not separable. Without governance, no enterprise should put an agent live. Without agents that outperform humans, governance is just paperwork. We have built a foundation and are continuing to invest in both at the same time. That's what a platform is.\n\n## **What it looks like when it works**\n\n**Amazon Ring** evaluated dozens of vendors but decided on Vapi and went to production in two weeks. Today, every inbound call to one of the most demanding consumer support operations in the world runs through Vapi. Even more impressive, CSAT went up. Jason Mitura, VP of Software Development, said it simply: “A lot of AI tools promise great outcomes. Vapi has delivered on them.”\n\n**Kavak**, the largest used-car marketplace in Latin America, made a company-wide bet on agents. Their CPO, Alejandro, went to the CEO and pitched a rebuild of every workflow \\- sales, operations, support \\- around voice AI, with the entire company either building or tuning agents. They started with one use case. They now run dozens. They built memory and personalization on top of our platform themselves, so a returning customer picks up exactly where they left off. We didn't ship that. They did; that is the power of our platform. Their call center became a revenue center. They doubled revenue in their Mexico market.\n\n**Instawork** moved candidate interviews from humans to agents. Supply doubled. The agent never has a bad day, so every candidate gets the same clean interview, whether at 2 pm or 2 am. Some candidates stay on for thirty minutes just to talk about their lives.\n\nA million developers have built on Vapi. Millions of agents have been created. We've handled more than a billion calls. We did almost no marketing to get there. The product is just that good, and the word spread.\n\nIn every one of these cases, the same thing happens: customers stop noticing. The business, on the other end of the line, starts to feel like a human.\n\n## **What this round funds**\n\nWith this round, we are focusing our investment in three places. **Distribution**, so the enterprises that should be evaluating us are evaluating us. **Delivery**, so customers go from \"we want to do this\" to \"we are doing this\" in weeks instead of quarters. And the engineering investment that matters most \\- **core infrastructure, governance, and the self-improvement loop** that turns every call into the agent's next training signal.\n\nWe are continuing to focus on building the parts that actually let enterprises ship with confidence. With tools like Composer, Monitoring, and Simulations \\- launched over the past few months \\- customers can close the loop between building an agent, testing it against reality, and adapting it when reality pushes back. You can watch every call. You can catch the failure before your customer does. \n\nThe end state is a platform where the agent that picks up the phone tomorrow is reliably better than the one that picked up the phone today. We are building toward that, every day, at every layer.\n\n## **The big claim**\n\nThere is a generational company to be built in voice. \n\nThree trillion minutes a year of business-to-customer voice. A category Twilio served for fifteen years and barely scratched. The biggest cost center in the Fortune 500, sitting there, waiting to become a revenue driver, and almost nobody is in the room.\n\nBut we are. We are building the platform that makes every business human.\n\nIf you want to spend the next few years on the most consequential thing you can do in AI right now, [come build it with us](https://vapi.ai/careers).\n\nA billion calls in, and we’re just getting started.\n\n— Jordan"])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"4f:[\"$\",\"div\",null,{\"className\":\"min-h-[50vh] bg-[#f2f0ed]\",\"data-nav-theme\":\"light\",\"children\":[[\"$\",\"$L53\",null,{\"data\":{\"@context\":\"https://schema.org\",\"@type\":\"BlogPosting\",\"headline\":\"AGI is here. Not every conversation belongs on a phone call. Password resets, order lookups, anything that ends with a link or a code: chat handles these well because the user can re-read, copy, and click to reach a swift resolution without leaving their interface. If the resolution is a URL, a code, or a number, chat is the right channel, and trying to bring those types of interactions to voice can be the reason a use case fails in the first place. \n\nVoice earns its place when the problem is urgent, hard to type, sophisticated, or even emotionally loaded. A patient describing symptoms, a customer disputing a charge, a driver who can't use their hands. These callers want to explain the problem in their own words and get it resolved in one conversation, especially when the resolution might not be so straightforward. Picking which use cases move to voice is half the work, and it should happen before anyone writes a prompt.\n\nOnce you've picked the right one, your chat scripts are a real asset. They encode your business logic, your edge cases, and years of tuning. But they're written for eyes and a cursor, and calls go to ears. This requires different media, each with its own rules and criteria for success. If a team copies and pastes its best-performing chat flows into a system prompt without recognizing the nuances that make a voice agent perform well, it could affect conversions, transfer rates, and other critical bottom-line metrics for your brand. Even if they have proven successful for chat, they were written to be read, not heard. Designing for the ear is its own discipline. Here are some tips and tricks for getting the most out of designing voice flows. \n\n#### **Split paragraphs into turns**\nThe spoken word is only present for a moment before it dissipates, and the flows must be created to reflect this. While chat tolerates a paragraph of context before the question, on a call, this is different, and the caller has forgotten the context by the time the question arrives. Break every long passage into turns that carry one idea or one question each, and put the important part first so you can ask the question while you still have their attention.\nSay \"Would Thursday at 2 pm work?\" Not \"I found availability on Thursday, and it looks like 2 pm is open, so would you like me to go ahead and book that for you?\" If you share too much information and are not intentional about how you share it, you might not just waste context; you might lose the person on the other end of the line. \n#### **Add the memory back in**\nWhile chat has a scroll bar, the voice medium does not. The date your script collected three steps ago is still on screen in chat and can easily be retrieved in a few moments, so the script does not need to repeat. A caller cannot scroll back, so there is a greater need for both repetition and context. That means your appointment booking must include that context and ask: \"Should I book Thursday, January 15th at 2 pm?\" instead of \"Should I go ahead and book that?\" Find every place in your chat flow that refers back to earlier input, and make the agent say the value out loud, including dates, times, or other critical context that might be forgotten or disregarded from earlier moments in the conversation. \n#### **Compress your option lists**\nA chat script can present five locations or four appointment slots because the user can scan them. Users have more time and can process more information for the potential options that they can take. When people are told information out loud, they hold and consider two or three options and not much more. Read four time slots aloud, and callers ask you to repeat them. If you offer two, they will pick one. Give fewer viable options, and customers can assess them and choose what suits them best. Turn lists into narrowing questions: \"I have openings Thursday afternoon or Friday morning. Which works better?\" Keep the rest in reserve. You can break up choices into multiple questions or offer fewer options so they can select the one best suited to them. \n#### **Confirm slots as you collect them**\nChat flows often gather everything and show a summary card at the end, which works because the user can review it. Visual aids can be added, and the customer has time to evaluate the decisions made. The spoken version of that summary is a string of five details the caller won't catch an error in. When spoken all at the same time, it can be difficult to synthesize and assess all the information confirmed on the call. Instead, when using voice, echo each critical slot the moment you collect it, when it is fresh in your mind. For example, when you are confirming a date and time, \"Got it, January 15th.\" One staffing company, for example, applied this to availability and certification questions and cut downstream placement errors by 30%.\n#### **Constrain your open questions**\n\"What would you like to change?\" works in chat, where the user can type a precise answer. A user can think and type out a thoughtful response that can then be analyzed. Spoken, open questions produce open answers, which in turn produce more clarifying questions. They can lead to more edge cases and often push resolution further away than it was at the beginning of the call. Turn them into choices that make deterministic paths based on their response: \"Would you like to reschedule to a different date, or cancel?” One team made this single swap and took 40 seconds off the average call duration. This makes calls more straightforward and increases overall resolution rates. \n#### **Add retry ceilings**\nChat rarely mishears, since the text can be referenced and, if needed, re-referenced. It does not have to deal with pauses, accents, and mispronunciations. Voice, on the other hand, is a different medium. In some cases, the transcription might mishear and could turn \"fifteen\" into \"fifty.\" Your chat scripts have no retry logic because they never needed it: the words are there for continued reference. Your voice agent needs a ceiling: ask normally, then rephrase with a format hint (\"Could you say the date as month and day? For example, January fifteenth\"), then escalate gracefully. Three attempts, then a human: this allows a graceful resolution if the call is not handled the first time perfectly, and allows opportunities for the information to be shared, without immediate human escalation. \n#### **Move the links**\nAny place your chat script ends with a URL or a reference code is a place your voice script should say, \"I'm going to send you a link by text so you don't have to write it down.\" Never read a URL aloud. It is unlikely that a link will be remembered during a live conversation. To share a link, it is much easier for a customer to click through an email or chat than to transcribe it or type it in. If a flow is mostly links, it probably should've stayed in chat. If only one link is needed, connect a tool to send it via email or text. \n#### **Then read it aloud**\nThe cheapest test in voice design costs nothing. Before you ship a converted flow, read it aloud. If you run out of breath on a turn, the caller will too.\nThis post draws on chapter 9 of the [Voice Agent Playbook](https://vapi.ai/playbook/design#chapter-9-conversation-design-fundamentals), which covers conversation design in full, including the pre-launch checklist."])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"5e:T2129,"])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"## Introduction\nThe Vapi homepage runs 15 voice agents covering 3 use cases across 5 languages. To build these, we did not hand-build them one by one in the dashboard. We started from a rough draft to scaffolding our entire fleet of agents before fine-tuning the results. This post gives you the framework we use to build faster, production-ready agents.\n## Agent fleets; programmatically\nFor the [Vapi homepage](https://vapi.ai/), we needed the same set of scenarios across multiple languages, which means that every time the script changes, every variant needs to change with it. Hand editing all of these introduces human error, drift, and is time consuming. Bootstrapping a fleet of agents in code allows you to move fast and iterate effectively.\n\nTo solve this, we generate the agents.\n## What you will leave with\n- A framework for building and iterating on agents in production based on how we build at Vapi\n- A skill that scaffolds the whole project from a rough draft\n- The configuration for the live agents running on the Vapi homepage\n\u003e **Note:** Just want to run the homepage agents as is? [Clone the repo](https://github.com/VapiAI/homepage-voice-agents/tree/main), add your `VAPI_PRIVATE_KEY`, then `bun run bootstrap`. That repo is the hardened end state of the framework below.\n## The framework\nThere are four phases: plan, draft, bootstrap, harden.\n\n### Phase 0: Plan\n\nPlanning is a cross-functional activity. For the homepage, this was a collaboration with marketing, product, sales, and leadership, resulting in three scenarios: `appointment-scheduling`, `qualification-screening`, `customer-support`, and five languages: `en`, `es`, `it`, `fr`, and a `multi` variant that handles 60+ languages in one call. Consider who your experts are in what the final agents should feel like and be able to do. The output of this phase will feed the draft and should cover what scenarios, languages, and details about the voice agent itself.\n\n### Phase 1: One rough draft as the single input\n\nThe single source of truth is one file, `ROUGH_DRAFT.md`. This is the source of truth that the fleet of agents will be generated from.\n\nStructure:\n- `scenario_name`\n- Opening line (**On the page** / **Opening**)\n- Short what-happens paragraph\n\n![rough-draft.png](https://ethical-reward-0125f27c94.media.strapiapp.com/rough_draft_631a02387c.png)\n\nThe structure of this draft is important, as it will map deterministically to the configuration:\n- Scenario name -\u003e derived snake-case `scenarioId`, which becomes the env var that holds the assistant id\n- Opening line -\u003e `firstMessage`\n- What happens -\u003e body.md\n\u003e **Note:** In our homepage agents, we later refined the ID to append `_ID` as a suffix. The conventions you choose are up to you.  \n\n### Phase 2: Bootstrapping\n\nUse the skill pointing at the `ROUGH_DRAFT.md`, and it will scaffold the whole project, including a small TypeScript spine, which is a per-language voice/transcriber stack, a prompt composer, a scenario registry, an assistant builder, and the bootstrap entry point. Run `bun run bootstrap` to generate your agent fleet.\n\n![bootstrap.png](https://ethical-reward-0125f27c94.media.strapiapp.com/bootstrap_ad1e5776e0.png)\n\nWhat the skill ships as defaults:\n- Two languages out of the box, `en` + `es`. Adding a third is one entry in each language record.\n- Model: OpenAI `gpt-4.1` at a flat temperature of 0.5, set once in `buildAssistant.ts`.\n- Voice: ElevenLabs `eleven_turbo_v2` (EN) / `eleven_multilingual_v2` (ES).\n- Transcriber: Deepgram `nova-3` (EN) / Soniox `stt-rt-v4` (ES).\n- `loadPrompt` composition: one `body.md` per scenario drives every language. EN returns the body unchanged; ES prepends a Spanish preamble with the scenario's localized off-topic redirects spliced in. One wording change to `body.md` re-applies to all variants.\n- Idempotent upsert loop and env-var-ID state model: for each (scenario x language) tuple, the script reads the assistant's id from an environment variable. Id set runs `assistants.update(id, body)`; not set runs `assistants.create(body)` and prints the new id. State lives in `.env.local`, so reruns are safe, and a stale id (deleted assistant, or a different org after a key rotation) falls back to create on a `404`.\n- \"Run it twice\" verification: the first run creates the fleet and prints the ids to paste into `.env.local`; the second run finds them and updates in place instead of duplicating.\nThe skill stops here, as the generated `body.md` is persona driven and handled in the next phase.\n### Phase 3: Harden the rough agents\nBootstrapping speeds up development, but the agents are still rough. This phase is the human-in-the-loop phase to refine your agents for production. Here you can:\n- **Add more languages.** The homepage extended `en` + `es` to five languages.\n- **Tune voice and model.** Per-scenario temperatures replaced the flat 0.5 (customer-support runs cooler at 0.4; the demo scenarios hotter). EN voices moved to per-scenario overrides with low stability (0.2) for warmth; non-EN sits at 0.5 with a `multi` fallback plan (OpenAI `tts-1`, then Cartesia `sonic-3`). The EN transcriber was swapped from `nova-3` to Deepgram `flux-general-en` with tuned end-of-turn thresholds; non-EN kept Soniox with a Deepgram `nova-3` fallback. A brand-vocabulary list keeps product names from being misheard.\n- **Persona becomes contract.** The rough `body.md` files grew hard-constraint, identity/security, and \"hard off-topic / chaos handling\" sections, plus localized `off-topic-\u003clang\u003e.md` redirect lines. This is where guardrails and off-ramps get added. Natural variation comes from the prompt itself via disfluency vocabulary, laughter rules, and banter sections.\n- **Capture tools.** Each scenario gained one async client tool.\n- **Analysis plans.** Each scenario ships an `analysisPlan` with a `summaryPlan` (always summarize in English, whatever language the call was in) and a `structuredDataPlan` that extracts a typed JSON record. For example, qualification's `follow_up_intent_score` on a 0 to 10 rubric, plus name, company, and use case.\n- **Hooks.** Customer-support added an idle hook (`cs_idle_topic_suggest`) that fires on `customer.speech.timeout` after about 12s and speaks a prompt from `idle-hook.md`.\n## Approaching iteration\nOnce your agent fleet is live, this framework allows for fast and effective iteration. To make changes, edit the source manually or prompt what changes you want in your favorite coding agent pointed to your repo, then re-run `bun run bootstrap`. This runs an upsert based on the stored assistant ids, so it will not duplicate your agents. A deleted or stale id will fall back to a fresh create.\nExample updates:\n- Change what an agent says: edit the `body.md` once and this reapplies to all agents.\n- Change one agent's voice or transcriber: edit that language's entry in `languages.ts`.\n- Tweak one scenario's voice: add a `voiceOverride` on the scenario.\n- Change the model or temperature: update the scenario's model config.\n\nYou can also grow the scenarios if you have a new use case after you go live.\n- Add a scenario: a `body.md`, a `scenarios/\u003cid\u003e.ts`, and register it in the scenario registry and id types.\n- Add a language: an id in the types, a voice and transcriber entry in `languages.ts`, and a shared language section or preamble.\nThe important thing to remember is to keep the bootstrap as the source of truth. If you make an edit in the dashboard, the next run will overwrite the edits.\n## Patterns to remember\n1. Bootstrap as code.\n2. One body per scenario, layer languages on top of this.\n3. Language drives your voice/transcriber, and the scenario drives the prompt, tools, and final configuration.\n4. The skill speeds up the beginning of your dev workflow; you do the final tuning.\n5. Natural variation is tuned in your prompt.\n6. Async tools keep calls moving.\n7. Analysis plans turn into structured data.\n## Resources and next steps\n- Try out the new homepage agents for yourself. [Run the new homepage agents](https://github.com/VapiAI/homepage-voice-agents/tree/main)  \n- Ready to build your own? Use the  [skill to start bootstrapping your own scenarios.](https://github.com/VapiAI/skills/blob/main/vapi-bootstrap-framework/SKILL.md)    \n- Visit our docs to learn more about [prompting for voice](https://docs.vapi.ai/prompting-guide) as you tune your agents.  \n- [Join us in the community](https://discord.gg/v5Ee6FhAZt) to share your expertise and connect with other voice agent developers."])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"5f:T1c8e,"])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"When your voice agents go to production, someone has to watch them. At a small scale, that person is usually close to the code. They know what the agents do; they catch something off in a support ticket and fix it before it becomes a pattern. But even then, figuring out what actually went wrong, who owns it, and how to resolve it without pulling focus from everything else they're building is a problem in itself.\n\nVapi has always given you the building blocks: structured outputs, logs, and the ability to connect to external tools. But operationalizing those required engineering time, which meant the ops team, the person actually accountable for production stability, was dependent on engineers to get visibility into what was running. \n\nAs you scale, that dependency compounds. Your agents are running hundreds or thousands of calls a day, and at that volume, you can only ever review a sample manually. Even if you are using a monitoring solution, once you uncover an issue, it can be difficult to identify what is wrong and resolve it accordingly. There's always a tradeoff between how much you catch and how fast you catch and resolve it. \n\nTeams find out something is wrong when a customer complains or a metric slips. Either way, the pattern is the same: you catch what you catch, and anything that falls between reviews stays broken until the next one.\n\nToday we're releasing Vapi Monitoring to change that. Not to replace the tools your ops and engineering teams already use, but to give ops teams the voice-specific visibility and resolution context they couldn't get without an engineer in the loop.\n\n## What we built\n\nWith Monitoring, you can create customizable monitors to ensure your agents are working exactly as you intend, and apply them to as many agents as you want. To set one up, select the type of monitor, describe what you want to track, and Vapi creates it for you. You choose when to be alerted about what monitoring finds, up to live for enterprise subscriptions.\n\nThe monitor defines what to observe. The threshold is how you manage noise: when a threshold is hit, you get alerted, Vapi creates an issue and tracks every call that meets your criteria, so your team can see a pattern rather than chase individual call failures. \n\nThis is what reduces MTTD. The monitoring dashboard organizes issues by type so you can immediately see which failed, how many calls were affected, and whether the problem is still active or has been resolved on its own.\n\nFrom there, each issue helps diagnose the issue and connects you to a resolution path that carries enough context for your team to triage fast: is this worth acting on now, given everything else going on, and if so, who owns it? That's the MTTR problem, and it's where most teams lose the most time. If you already use external monitoring tools, Monitoring works alongside them, adding the voice-specific context they can't provide on their own and recommending a resolution.\n\n### What gets monitored\n\n**Effectiveness monitoring** tracks whether your agents are actually doing their job. That means intent fulfillment, whether the call accomplished what the agent's prompt defined as success, early hang-ups, and when something isn't working, a path to resolution, so you're not just staring at a failure with no next step. Available for Enterprise subscriptions.\n\n**Compliance monitoring** tracks whether your agents are following the instructions and constraints defined in their prompts. Failures here aren't just a product problem; they're a liability exposure. Available for Enterprise subscriptions.\n\n**Technical monitoring** covers system integrations, typically tools: tool call failures, provider failures across STT, LLM, and TTS, failover and degraded mode activations, and assistant request failures. When issues are detected, you get enough context to identify what broke and how to fix it without leaving the platform.\n\n**Infrastructure monitoring** covers behavior within the external call pipeline: latency, dropped calls, and when concurrency or API limits are reached.\n\nThe line between these tiers is meaningful. Technical and infrastructure monitoring tells you the platform is operating correctly and helps provide solutions when things break. Maybe you add a new tool. You test a few calls in the playground, everything looks great, and you deploy. A week later, you realize your assistant stopped offering financing on half the relevant calls. Nothing crashed. Nothing alerted. Conversions just quietly dropped.\n\nThe problem is not that you made a bad change. The problem is that you had no way to know.\n\n## How We Got Here\n\nRight now, most teams test assistants the same way: replay a few calls, skim some transcripts, decide it feels good enough. This works fine when your agent is simple. It stops working the moment you have continuous prompt changes, new tools, or model swaps.\n\nThe failures that hurt most are the silent ones. Your assistant stops collecting required information. It calls a tool with the wrong arguments. It forgets to mention the 60-month term on financing offers. These regressions only show up days later in metrics or, worse, anecdotal reports from your sales team.\n\nCode has tests. Prompts and tools do not. That is the gap.\n\n## Turn-Based Evals\n\nToday we are shipping Evals, a way to write tests for your voice agents that run the same way your unit tests do.\n\nThe core idea is simple. You define an eval as a JSON conversation that simulates a call. For each important assistant turn, you attach a judge plan that specifies exactly what must happen: the text it should produce, the tool it should call, the arguments it should pass.\n\nHere is what an eval looks like for a service appointment booking flow:\n\n```\n{\n  \"name\": \"Book service appointment\",\n  \"name\": \"Book service appointment\",\n  \"type\": \"chat.mockConversation\",\n  \"messages\": [\n    { \"role\": \"user\", \"content\": \"I need to service my 2021 Hatchback\" },\n    {\n      \"role\": \"assistant\",\n      \"judgePlan\": {\n        \"model\": {\n          \"provider\": \"openai\",\n          \"model\": \"gpt-4o\",\n          \"messages\": [\n            {\n              \"role\": \"system\",\n              \"content\": \"You are an expert evaluator. You can ONLY return pass or fail and NOTHING else. Look at the assistant message and evaluate it based on the following criteria:\\n\\nPass criteria: The assistant message should be asking the user for their contact information\\n\\nFail criteria:  Return fail if the assistant does not do the things mentioned above\"\n            },\n            {\n              \"role\": \"user\",\n              \"content\": \"The assistant message is: {{messages[-1]}}\"\n            }\n          ]\n        }\n      }\n    },\n    { \"role\": \"user\", \"content\": \"Alex Lee, 555-0134\" },\n    { \"role\": \"assistant\", \"content\": \"What's the current mileage?\" },\n    { \"role\": \"user\", \"content\": \"30,000 miles\" },\n    {\n      \"role\": \"assistant\",\n      \"judgePlan\": {\n        \"judgeType\": \"exact\",\n        \"toolCalls\": [\n          {\n            \"name\": \"get_current_mileage\",\n            \"arguments\": {\n              \"lastName\": \"Lee\",\n              \"phoneNumber\": \"555-0134\",\n              \"currentMileage\": \"30,000 miles\"\n            }\n          }\n        ]\n      }\n    }\n  ]\n}\n\n```\n\nYou run this eval locally while iterating on prompts. You wire the same eval into your CI/CD pipeline. If the assistant stops asking for scheduling or fails to call the calendar tool, the build fails before anything hits production.\n\n## What You Can Test\n\nEvals support three judging strategies, each suited to different kinds of checks.\n\nExact matching works for deterministic behaviors. Use regex patterns when the assistant must mention specific terms, or JSON matching when a tool call must include particular arguments. You can ignore dynamic fields like timestamps or IDs so your Evals stay stable.\n\nLLM-as-judge handles the fuzzy stuff. Tone, empathy, safety, policy adherence. You write a judging prompt that describes what you expect, and the judge returns a pass or fail. No more hand-writing brittle regexes for subjective behaviors.\n\nTool call verification tests the full loop. Assert that the assistant calls the right tool with the right arguments. Check that tool responses match expected patterns. Override tool responses and continue the conversation to test downstream behavior even when tools are dynamic.\n\n## In Practice\n\nUnityAI's engineering team has been using Evals to validate LLM logic before running full simulations. They've caught tool calls firing with extra parameters, tools not being called when expected, and prompt contradictions that would have been invisible in manual testing.\n\nThe pattern: run Evals first to confirm the LLM is handling logic correctly, then do deeper simulation testing for edge cases. Developers don't want to manually call every time to test prompts. Evals give them a fast check to see if things are working, then they go deeper.\n\n## From Call Logs to Tests\n\nThe best Evals come from production issues you have already seen.\n\nWhen you discover a bad call in your logs, you can turn that transcript into a test. In the dashboard, pull up the call, click the thumbs down button to use it as an eval, specify what the assistant should have done instead, and save. That issue becomes a concrete test that guards against regression forever.\n\n![Screenshot 2025-12-03 at 10.45.29 AM.png](https://ethical-reward-0125f27c94.media.strapiapp.com/Screenshot_2025_12_03_at_10_45_29_AM_69cdda0057.png)\n\nThis is the loop that makes agents reliable over time. Every production failure becomes a new constraint that gets checked on every future change.\nBatch runs and CI/CD\nIndividual Evals are useful. Running multiple Evals makes them powerful.\n\nWith batch runs, you can execute multiple Evals at once: all your financing checks, appointment flows, and compliance behaviors. Developers choose which Evals to run for each pipeline, so you can tailor coverage to the changes you’re shipping.\n\nThe CLI runs the same Evals you define in the dashboard. Wire it into your pipeline with a single command. The output is machine-readable, so you can plug it into whatever CI system you already use.\n\nYou can set up your flow so that if any blocking eval fails, your build stops. Your prompts get the same discipline as your code.\n\n\n```\nconst response = await fetch(`https://api.vapi.ai/eval/run`, {\n method: \"POST\",\n headers: {\n   Authorization: `Bearer ${VAPI_API_KEY}`,\n   \"Content-Type\": \"application/json\",\n },\n body: JSON.stringify({\n   type: \"eval\",\n   // Create an Eval with everything you want to test for in the new assistant\n   eval: {\n     \"type\": \"chat.mockConversation\",\n     \"messages\": [...],\n   },\n   target: {\n     type: \"assistant\",\n     // Pass a transient assistant with the new assistant's settings before publishing it to production\n     assistant: {...},\n   },\n }),\n});\n\n\nconst result = await response.json();\nconst evalRunId = result.id;\nlet evalRunCompleted = false;\nlet evalRunResult;\n\n\nwhile (!evalRunCompleted) {\n const evalRun = await fetch(`https://api.vapi.ai/eval/run/${evalRunId}`, {\n   method: \"GET\",\n   headers: {\n     Authorization: `Bearer ${VAPI_API_KEY}`,\n   },\n });\n evalRunResult = await evalRun.json();\n evalRunCompleted = evalRunResult?.status === \"completed\";\n await new Promise(resolve =\u003e setTimeout(resolve, 5000));\n}\n\n\nif(evalRunResult.results[0].status === \"pass\") {\n console.log(\"Eval passed\");\n} else {\n console.log(\"Eval failed\");\n}\n\n```\n\n## What This Changes\n\nThe developer experience shifts from hope to confidence.\n\n**Before**: you change a prompt, test it manually, deploy, and wait to see if something breaks. \n\n**After**: you change a prompt, run your eval suite, see exactly which turns passed or failed, fix the issues, and deploy knowing you have not regressed critical behaviors.\n\nTech leads get a quick signal before release. QA gets reproducible, versioned tests. Prompt engineers get precise guardrails. Backend engineers get the deterministic checks they expect from the rest of their stack.\n\nYour agents become something you can trust to behave consistently, even as prompts change, tools evolve, and models get swapped.\n\n## Get Started\n\nEvals are available now. You can create them from the Evals page, programmatically via the API, or conveniently via the call logs page.\n\nStart with a handful of critical behaviors: financing offers, appointment booking, required disclosures, transfers to humans. Instead of cramming every scenario into a single prompt, you can compose specialized assistants that hand off conversations while maintaining context. You decide what each assistant handles, how they hand off, and what context to share. Together, these specialists handle complexity that would break any single assistant.\n\n![Squads Builder Overview](https://ethical-reward-0125f27c94.media.strapiapp.com/Screenshot_2025_11_01_at_5_30_26_PM_a7dd8fa6ca.png)\n\n# Why we built this\n\nEvery voice AI developer is familiar with this progression. You start with a simple assistant that books appointments. It works well. Then the Product asks for payment processing. Then customer service. Then order tracking.\n\nYour once-clean prompt becomes thousands of conflicting instructions. The assistant that used to book appointments reliably now confuses Tuesday with Thursday because somewhere deep in the prompt, you added logic for handling refunds.\n\nThe existing approaches all have problems:\n\nSingle mega-prompts become unmaintainable and unreliable as complexity grows.\n\nMultiple phone numbers fragment the customer experience and confuse users.\n\nExternal orchestration introduces latency, drops calls, and adds another failure point.\n\nWorkflow tools from other providers conceal the routing logic, making debugging nearly impossible when issues arise.\n\nMeanwhile, companies like Fleetworks need to handle dispatch, scheduling, billing, and support within a single conversation. One prompt can't handle this elegantly or reliably. Today, Fleetworks runs 240,000 calls a day through Squads. It's remarkable to see something that started as a sketch during a product meeting now orchestrating nearly a quarter million conversations daily, handling the exact complexity that would break any single assistant.\n\n# How Squads work\n\nSquads enable you to build specialized assistants that excel in one area each. A greeting agent qualifies and routes the caller. A scheduling agent books appointments. A support agent handles complaints. They pass control silently and share precisely the context needed.\n\n## Visual flow design\n\nThe Squad builder provides a canvas where you design conversation flows visually. You connect assistants with routing logic and see how calls will flow through them. Each node represents an assistant, each edge represents a potential handoff.\n\n![Greeting Assistant flow](https://ethical-reward-0125f27c94.media.strapiapp.com/Screenshot_2025_11_01_at_5_30_56_PM_670a380b01.png)\n\nAs you map out your flows, you'll face a design choice: how should assistants connect to each other? You could create direct paths between every specialist, but that quickly becomes a tangled web. \n\nA cleaner approach that many teams choose: use one assistant as your traffic controller. After your greeting, route calls through this central assistant, which determines the caller's needs and directs them to the appropriate specialist. Think of it like a receptionist who knows exactly which department handles what. Instead of building a maze where every specialist needs to know about every other specialist, everything flows through this smart routing point. When specialists finish their task, they send callers back to ask, \"anything else I can help with?\" This keeps your Squad organized, no matter how many specialists you add.\n\n## Context control per handoff\n\nFor each handoff between assistants, you control what context passes through:\n\n**None** for fresh starts when switching to sensitive domains like payments\n\n**Last N messages** when you need just enough context to continue\n\n**All messages** when full conversation history matters\n\nThis isn't a global setting. Each handoff can have different context rules based on what makes sense for that specific transition.\n\n![Context configuration](https://ethical-reward-0125f27c94.media.strapiapp.com/Screenshot_2025_11_01_at_5_23_01_PM_3146cbb3ff.png)\n\n## Seamless transitions\n\nThe handoff happens without audio artifacts. Multiple specialized assistants work together behind the scenes. Your customers experience a single, coherent interaction, while you reap the benefits of a modular design.\n\n## Control where it matters\n\nWith Squads, you control the routing prompts sent to LLM.\n\nWhen your greeting assistant needs to decide whether to transfer a customer to support or sales, you write the exact prompt and tools that are sent to the LLM. Test it against other models.\n\nThe best model is the one that works well with your use case."])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"6b:T16c2,"])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"Building a voice agent that can navigate a phone menu might seem easy.\u0026nbsp;\n\nYou generate a tone, the system hears it, and the call moves forward.\n\nWell, it's not that simple. One of our forward-deployed engineers, [Steven](https://www.linkedin.com/in/stevenbdf/), was working with an enterprise customer trying to get their agent deployed.\u0026nbsp;\n\nTheir use case involved navigating IVR menus across five different providers, and the unreliability was killing their success rates.\u0026nbsp;\n\nThe failing DTMF tones led to longer call durations and frustrated end-users.\n\nAfter countless hours of debugging failed call flows and frustrated user reports, we mapped out the core issues.\u0026nbsp;\n\nIt comes down to 3 things:\u0026nbsp;\n\n![](/blog/images/how-we-solved-dtmf-reliability-in-voice-ai-systems/why-dtmf-hard.png)\n\n## **The 3 Ways DTMF Can Go Wrong**\n\n### Problem #1: Mangled Audio\n\nVoice calls run on codecs like Opus or G.711, which are built to compress human speech. They use psychoacoustic models that prioritize the frequencies in our voice (roughly 300-3400 Hz) and discard what the human ear doesn't perceive as critical.\n\nA DTMF tone however is not speech. It's a precise combination of 2 pure sine waves.\u0026nbsp;\n\nFor the digit \"1\", it's exactly 697 Hz and 1209 Hz. When a codec compresses this signal, it quantizes, filters, and distorts these pure frequencies.\u0026nbsp;\n\nThe harmonics shift, the phase relationship breaks. To the receiving system, the tone becomes an unrecognizable smudge of audio. The result is a failed input.\n\n### **Problem #2: The Network is Unreliable**\n\nVoice packets travel over public networks. This means packet loss, jitter, and bandwidth fluctuations are unavoidable.\u0026nbsp;\n\nDTMF detection algorithms, often based on Goertzel or FFT approaches, need a clean, consistent signal for at least 40-50ms to confirm a digit.\n\nJitter reorders packets, creating gaps in the tone. Packet loss deletes parts of it entirely.\u0026nbsp;\n\nA receiving IVR might hear a garbled signal, nothing at all, or misinterpret a \"11\" as a \"7\".\u0026nbsp;\n\nThis is especially true for legacy IVR systems that are notoriously unforgiving.\n\n### **Problem #3: Every Provider is a Special Case**\n\nYes, there's a standard for sending DTMF out-of-band: RFC 2833. It defines sending the DTMF event in a separate RTP payload, bypassing the audio stream entirely.\u0026nbsp;\n\nIn a perfect world, everyone would use it, and this blog post wouldn't exist.\n\nThe problem is, production isn't perfect. The real world is a patchwork of legacy IVR systems, custom telephony setups, and carrier-specific interpretations.\n\nWe found that:\n\n- Many older IVR systems don't support RFC 2833 and only listen for in-band audio tones.\n- Among providers that do support the standard, implementation details like timings, payload formats, and acknowledgment mechanisms vary just enough to cause silent failures.\n- Other providers use entirely different methods, like SIP INFO messages.\n\nAn approach that works perfectly on one provider fails on another. This creates a compatibility matrix from hell for any developer.\u0026nbsp;\n\n![](/blog/images/how-we-solved-dtmf-reliability-in-voice-ai-systems/journey-to-dtmf.png)\n\n## **Our Journey to a Solution**\n\n### **The First Attempt: Simple Audio Generation**\n\nWe started with the obvious approach: generate DTMF tones as audio and send them through the voice stream. We carefully crafted each tone using the exact frequencies:\n\n- \"1\" = 697 Hz + 1209 Hz\n- \"2\" = 697 Hz + 1336 Hz\n- \"3\" = 697 Hz + 1477 Hz\n\nAnd so on...\n\nThis worked on localhost. It worked in a clean network. But it failed inconsistently in production. The combination of codec mangling and network noise made it too unreliable for real-world use.\n\n### **The Second Attempt: Use Provider APIs**\n\nNext, we used provider-native APIs to send DTMF digits out-of-band.\u0026nbsp;\n\nThis bypasses the audio stream entirely, avoiding compression issues.\n\nThis was a step forward, but reliability was still inconsistent. Some providers had robust APIs, others were flaky. Some didn't support it at all for certain call types.\u0026nbsp;\n\nWe had traded one set of problems for another.\n\n## **The Only Thing That Worked**\n\n![](/blog/images/how-we-solved-dtmf-reliability-in-voice-ai-systems/how-we-dtmf.png)\n\nWe realized there is no single silver bullet.\u0026nbsp;\n\nThe only solution is an intelligent, adaptive system that uses the best tool for the job on a per-call basis.\n\nHere is the architecture we built:\n\n- **Primary Path: Provider-Specific DTMF (RFC 2833 / API).** \\\n  When we’re on a call with a provider that has a reliable out-of-band DTMF API, we use it. This is the cleanest, most direct method. We built provider-specific adapters to handle the quirks of each API.\n- **Fallback Path: Codec-Aware Audio Synthesis.** \\\n  If the primary path is unavailable or fails, we fall back to generating audio. But we don't just generate a simple tone. Our synthesis engine is codec-aware. It generates tones at 16kHz with specific amplitude normalization designed to survive compression cycles with minimal distortion.\n\n## **The Results**\n\nBy abstracting this complexity away, we achieved predictable performance.\n\n- Provider API Method: \u003e90% success rate.\n- Audio Fallback Method: \u003e80% success rate.\n- Combined Hybrid System: \u003e93% overall success rate.\n\nUsers no longer get stuck in IVR loops. Our support queue for DTMF-related issues is nearly empty because the system now self-heals.\n\nDTMF is a perfect example of a problem that looks simple on the surface but hides immense technical depth. The \"right\" architecture isn't the most elegant one on a whiteboard but one that is a resilient, multi-layered system that works in the messy reality of production.\n\nWe're now applying this hybrid, adaptive model to other hard problems like voicemail detection and call transfers."])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"6c:T1f73,"])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"Background noise is a solved problem. Background speech is not.\n\nFor years, denoisers have successfully filtered out keyboard clicks and traffic.\u0026nbsp;\n\nBut there's a type of noise they are fundamentally designed to preserve: human speech.\n\nThis creates a paradox. When a user is on a call with a TV playing in the background, a standard denoiser does its job perfectly.\u0026nbsp;\n\nIt preserves the user's voice, *and* it preserves the voice of the news anchor.\n\nThe result is a garbled transcript and a confused agent.\u0026nbsp;\n\n![](/blog/images/how-we-built-adaptive-background-speech-filtering-at-vapi/denoiser-paradox.png)\n\n\\\nThis isn't a theoretical problem. The entire project started with one of our forward-deployed engineers, [Adi](https://www.linkedin.com/in/adithya-sairam/).\n\nAdi has worked with over a dozen enterprise customers to get their voice agents into production.\u0026nbsp;\n\nDuring one deployment, he hit a wall. The customer's agents were in an environment where TVs were often playing in the background.\u0026nbsp;\n\nEven with our standard Krisp-powered denoising, the assistant would pick up the TV's speech, derailing the conversation.\n\n[Krisp](https://krisp.ai/) was doing its job perfectly and was preserving human speech.\u0026nbsp;\n\nThe problem was, it couldn't tell the difference between the user and the news anchor. We needed a different approach.\n\n### **First we tried the most obvious path - Using AI**\n\nThe first impulse was to fight AI with more AI.\u0026nbsp;\n\nTrain a model to differentiate primary speaker from background media\u0026nbsp;\n\nWe considered it, but the costs were too high and it also introduced these challenges:\\\n![](/blog/images/how-we-built-adaptive-background-speech-filtering-at-vapi/ai-prblem-1.png)\n\nThe obvious solution might be to throw more machine learning at the problem. Train a model to distinguish between \"primary speaker\" and \"background media.\" We considered this, but it introduced several challenges:\n\n1. **Latency:** A new ML model adds processing time to our already tight sub-500ms latency budget.\n1. **Context Loss:** These models need several seconds of audio to work, making them useless for real-time turn-taking.\n1. **Cost:** More models mean more GPU usage, which means higher costs.\n\nThrowing another model at this was not the right way to do this.\n\nWe had to find a fundamental acoustic difference between a user speaking and a TV playing.\n\n### **The answer led us to signal analysis.**\u0026nbsp;\n\nBroadcast audio is heavily compressed.\u0026nbsp;\n\nIt has unique characteristics that human speech in a normal room does not.\n\nCharacteristics such as:\n\n- Consistent volume levels\n- Sustained energy patterns (meaning no natural pauses)\n- Predictable amplitude distribution\n\nWe built a system to detect these patterns mathematically and ..it worked.. sometimes.\n\nBut a fixed filter is brittle. A loud TV in a quiet room has a different acoustic profile than a quiet TV in a noisy call center.\\\nThe real problem wasn't just detecting media but also adapting to any environment in real-time.\n\n### **The breakthrough was the adaptive baseline.**\n\nInstead of a fixed threshold for \"noise,\" our system learns the acoustic profile of the environment on the fly through:\n\n1. **Rolling Window Analysis:** It maintains a 3-second rolling window of audio levels.\n1. **Percentile Calculation:** It finds the 85th percentile of speech volume to identify the primary speaker's level.\n1. **Dynamic Offset:** It filters audio that falls a specific amount (e.g., 15dB) below this moving baseline.\n\nThe baseline also updates every 20ms. If a user moves from a quiet room to a loud one, the filter adapts in seconds.\n\n### **The Media Detection Algorithm**\n\nThe last step was to automate the switch to a more aggressive mode when media is detected. Our algorithm looks for these telltale signs:\n\n- Variance \u003c 55dB (consistent volume)\n- Sustained moderate volume for \u003e 1 second\n- 85% of samples within a narrow range\n\nWhen these patterns are detected, the system automatically switches to more aggressive settings optimized for media filtering.\u0026nbsp;\n\nWhen the media is turned off, it gracefully returns to normal.\n\nWe call it **Fourier Denoising**, an experimental feature available today.\n\n### **How It Works**\n\nAll of this complexity is controlled by a single boolean.\n\n```typescript\nbackgroundSpeechDenoisingPlan: {\n  fourierDenoisingPlan: {\n    enabled: true,\n    mediaDetectionEnabled: true // The magic happens here\n  }\n}\n```\n\n\\\nWith `mediaDetectionEnabled: true`, the system:\n\n1. Monitors audio patterns in real-time\n1. Detects consistent media signatures (TV/radio/music)\n1. If you’re looking for more information on sampling rates and how they impact voice AI, you’re in the right place.\n\n## **Key Takeaways**\n\nSampling rate controls three key factors that significantly impact voice experiences: audio quality, response latency, and bandwidth costs. Higher rates capture more detail, but they also slow your pipeline and consume more data. Lower rates may feel snappier, but they risk losing critical speech information.\n\n16 kHz captures everything needed for clear speech recognition while keeping systems responsive and costs reasonable. This is why most voice assistants, cloud models, and Vapi default to 16 kHz.\n\n**Core principles:**\n\n- Match rates across your entire chain (microphone → Vapi → ASR → TTS).\n- Default to 16 kHz for speech applications.\n- Always respect the Nyquist criterion (sample rate ≥ 2 × target bandwidth).\n- Watch for mismatches that add processing time and degrade quality.\n\n## **Sampling Rate Explained**\n\nPicture your microphone tracing a sound wave. To digitize it, you *sample* at equal intervals, taking rapid-fire measurements. The pace is your *sampling rate*. At 16 kHz, you're capturing 16,000 snapshots per second.\n\n**Formula:** fs = samples taken / time interval (seconds)\n\nInside an ADC (analog-to-digital converter), each sample freezes the incoming voltage and writes it to memory. String those values together, and you get a discrete signal you can store, transmit, or feed into an automatic speech recognition engine. Those sample points are the only information your speech model will see, so their spacing matters.\n\n### **The Nyquist-Shannon Safeguard**\n\nThe [Nyquist-Shannon theorem](https://home.strw.leidenuniv.nl/~por/AOT2019/docs/AOT_2019_Ex13_NyquistTheorem.pdf) proves you must sample at least twice the highest frequency to rebuild the original wave without distortion. This Nyquist rate draws a hard line. Sample slower and high-frequency content folds back into lower bands as *aliasing*.\n\nEngineers define the Nyquist frequency as *fs/2,* which represents your trustworthy bandwidth ceiling. Speech tops out around 8 kHz. Following Nyquist, 16 kHz comfortably captures conversational nuances without overspending on bandwidth, which explains why most voice AI stacks settle on this frequency.\n\n**Key terms:**\n\n- **Sample:** Single voltage reading from the wave.\n- **Aliasing:** False artifacts when sampling below the Nyquist rate.\n- **Oversampling:** Capturing data well above the Nyquist rate to ease filtering.\n- **Bit depth:** Controls amplitude precision (separate from rate).\n\n## **Audio Sampling Rates \u0026 Use Cases**\n\nSelect the wrong audio sampling rate, and you'll chase problems through your entire voice pipeline. Pick the correct voice sampling rate and you balance fidelity, latency, and bandwidth in one stroke.\n\n{% table %}\n- **Rate**\n- **Applications**\n- **Purpose**\n---\n- 8 kHz\n- Legacy telephony, bandwidth-constrained bots\n- Speech up to 4 kHz. Intelligibility only\n---\n- **16 kHz**\n- **Voice assistants, ASR, VoIP**\n- **Sweet spot: covers the full speech band**\n---\n- 22.05 kHz\n- Low-bandwidth music, podcasts\n- Half CD quality, smaller files\n---\n- 44.1 kHz\n- Consumer music, high-quality podcasts\n- Full human hearing range\n---\n- 48 kHz\n- Film, broadcast, conferencing\n- Video sync, post-production headroom\n---\n- 96+ kHz\n- Studio recording, VR, archival\n- Heavy editing, spatial audio\n{% /table %}\n\nHuman speech spans roughly 85 Hz to 8 kHz. 16 kHz clears the Nyquist bar cleanly, explaining why [speech-to-text](https://vapi.ai/blog/what-is-speech-to-text) vendors default to it: [recognition accuracy plateaus](https://www.futurebeeai.com/blog/sample-rate-for-asr) beyond 16 kHz for everyday conversation.\n\nBut sometimes you need more nuance. Emotional prosody, whispered consonants, background music; 44.1 kHz captures details that 16 kHz misses. Tonal languages, such as Mandarin, contain pitch cues in low-frequency ranges, and a sampling rate of 16 kHz generally suffices without requiring excessive bandwidth.\n\nStart at 16 kHz, listen critically, then climb only when you hear something missing.\n\n## **Digital Audio Sampling: Quality vs. Latency vs. Bandwidth**\n\nPicking an audio sampling rate creates a three-way trade-off. Higher sample rates sound better but force more data through networks and add processing time, whereas lower rates feel snappier but risk muffled speech and recognition errors.\n\n**Data requirements (uncompressed 16-bit mono PCM):**\n\n- 8 kHz: ~128 kbps\n- 16 kHz: ~256 kbps\n- 48 kHz: ~768 kbps\n\nThese numbers pile up across thousands of concurrent sessions traveling both directions.\n\n**Where latency sneaks in:** Every extra kilobit gets captured, encoded, shipped, decoded, and fed to ASR or TTS. Staying inside that window often matters more than maximizing fidelity.\n\n## **Common Distortions \u0026 Fixes**\n\n**Aliasing** hits hardest. When you sample below the Nyquist rate, high-frequency energy folds back as ghost tones that mask consonants, creating a metallic quality. To fix it, use filters with a frequency of 16 kHz or higher, or employ anti-aliasing filters.\n\n**Aperture error** occurs when converters need a finite time per sample, blurring transients and making speech sound smeared. In this case, seek better hardware or higher rates.\n\n**Jitter** introduces timing randomness. Instead of arriving every 62.5 µs in 16 kHz streams, samples drift, creating hiss and phasing. Stable clocks and clock recovery are key here.\n\n**Robotic distortion** combines multiple issues. When your microphone outputs 48 kHz but WebRTC expects 16 kHz, continuous resampling creates \"chipmunk\" voices. Your ticket allows one free change. Would you like the 8:15 a.m. flight?\"\u0026nbsp;\n- At **0.9**, it says: \"Absolutely, let's get you on an earlier flight. An 8:15 a.m. departure is open, and I can waive the change fee. Sound good?\"\u0026nbsp;\n\nSame facts, different personality, all dependent on **LLM Temperature**. Temperature re-weights the probability distribution for each token your voice agent selects. Get it wrong and your agent either babbles off-brand or recites policy verbatim. Get it right and you strike the ideal balance between reliability, personality, and speed.\n\nHere we dive into LLM Temperature: what it is, why it matters, and how it works. With this information at your disposal, your next voice agent build will hit the right note.\u0026nbsp;\n\n**» [Test LLM temperature](https://vapi.ai/) on a voice agent right now.**\n\n## **What is LLM Temperature**\n\nLLM temperature is a sampling parameter that scales probabilities that an LLM assigns to each possible next token. Lower settings yield reliable but robotic answers, while higher settings encourage diversity, sometimes at the expense of precision.\n\nTechnically, temperature divides the logits before the softmax function is applied. A value near **0** sharpens the distribution so that top-ranked tokens dominate. Values above **1** flatten it, giving low-probability tokens a fighting chance.\n\n**P(i) = exp(logitᵢ / T) / Σ exp(logitⱼ / T)**\n\nFor voice agents, temperature is all about balance. A customer-support bot at **0.2** builds trust with consistent language. A storytelling companion at **0.9** keeps listeners engaged with spontaneity. Because voice interactions occur in real-time, users notice tonal shifts instantly.\n\nMost practitioners work within these ranges:\n\n- **0.0–0.3**: Deterministic responses for compliance-heavy exchanges\n- **0.4–0.7**: Balanced, natural conversation (safe default)\n- **0.8–1.2**: Creative, persuasive responses for brainstorming or entertainment\n- **1.3–2.0**: Experimental territory where originality spikes but reliability drops\n\n## **How LLM Temperature Works**\n\nEvery possible token receives a score (logit) reflecting its likelihood of coming next, and temperature reshapes this probability curve.\n\nConsider the prompt \"How can I reset my password?\" with logits of 2.0 for \"Click,\" 1.5 for \"Tap,\" and 1.0 for \"Navigate.\" At **T = 0.2**, \"Click\" dominates. At **T = 1.2**, \"Tap\" and \"Navigate\" appear much more often.\n\nIn Vapi's stack, this temperature lives in your agent configuration. Every runtime call scales logits by your chosen value, then streams audio back. Using the right providers makes LLM swapping trivial without requiring a rethinking of temperature strategy. Pairing with fast engines like Deepgram ensures that [temperature-driven responses remain perfectly in sync](https://docs.vapi.ai/providers/voice/deepgram).\n\nIf you use nucleus sampling (top-p), think of temperature as the macro lens and top-p as the zoom. Both trim the probability space, but temperature reshapes the whole curve while top-p chops off the tail.\n\n## **Why LLM Temperature Matters**\n\nTemperature shapes trust, brand consistency, and response time. In temperature tuning, we face a fundamental tension between reliability and creativity.\n\nLow settings (0.0-0.3) dramatically reduce hallucinations and ensure factual consistency, critical for agents associated with financial or medical advice. Accuracy climbs as temperature falls: higher settings [inject variability but risk drifting off-script](https://www.perfectapps.com/reducing-ai-hallucinations-with-temperature-settings-and-rag/).\n\nVoice is brand. A bank's agent with consistent phrasing bolsters identity, while a gaming companion's pop-culture riffs keep players engaged. In regulated environments, one rogue sentence can undo months of compliance work.\n\nHigh-creativity models tend to ramble. Lower settings keep the output concise, [producing tighter summaries](https://www.projectpro.io/article/llm-temperature/1073) that get to the point more quickly. In real-time conversations, milliseconds count, and broader token evaluation adds latency.\n\nMisaligned settings break everything. Near-zero values make sales agents feel robotic until callers disengage. Push past 1.0, and support bots might volunteer unsupported \"fixes,\" eroding credibility.\n\n**» Speak to a Vapi-powered [multilingual digital voice assistan](https://vapi.ai/custom-agents/multilingual-customer-service-agent)t.**\n\n## **How to Tune LLM Temperature**\n\nStart by defining your agent's role. Customer support rewards low variability; entertainment agents earn their keep by surprising listeners.\n\nThen, choose a baseline:\n\n- **0.0–0.3**: Factual delivery, FAQ flows where every word must ring true\n- **0.1–0.4**: Customer support that avoids sounding robotic\n- **0.5–0.7**: Sales and marketing with persuasive flair\n- **0.7–1.0**: Creative experiences where spontaneity matters most\n\nNow you need to test systematically. When you’re building with Vapi, you can [create two agent variants at different temperatures](https://docs.vapi.ai/customization/custom-llm/fine-tuned-openai-models) and route equal traffic to both. Classic A/B testing reveals whether users reward creativity or penalize drift.\n\nMake sure to log everything and store parameter values alongside transcripts. Tools like [AssemblyAI](https://docs.vapi.ai/providers/transcriber/assembly-ai) add word-level timestamps to spot where higher temperatures caused drift. For multilingual coverage, [Gladia](https://docs.vapi.ai/providers/transcriber/gladia) allows you to maintain the same settings while switching languages.\n\n**Watch for three red flags:**\n\n1. Repetitive phrasing – temperature is too low.\u0026nbsp;\n1. Factual slips – temperature is set too high.\n1. Latency spikes – wider probability consideration\n\nIn essence, if responses start to drift off topic, refine the prompt. If they stay on topic but feel too stiff or wild, tweak the temperature.\n\n**Practical tips:** Choose either temperature or top-p as your primary diversity lever (not both). Use staged rollouts, deploying new values to small traffic percentages first. Stay context-aware, as dynamic systems can adjust temperature within the same call.\n\n## Real World Examples\n\n1. **Customer Support:** \"I need help with my account.\"\n   1. **Temperature 0.2:** \"I can help with that. First, open the Vapi app and tap Settings \u003e Account. The 0.2 response sounds like a spec sheet, while 1.0 risks hyperbole your legal team never approved.\n\n## LLM Temperature Comparison\n\n{% table %}\n\n- **Temperature**\n- **Tone**\n- **Accuracy \u0026 Hallucination Risk**\n- **Creativity \u0026 Engagement**\n- **Ideal Voice Use Case**\n\n---\n\n- 0.2\n- Formal, concise\n- **High accuracy** • minimal risk\n- Low\n- Password resets, policy explanations\n\n---\n\n- 0.7\n- Conversational, balanced\n- Reliable with occasional flair\n- Balanced\n- Sales pitches, casual chat\n\n---\n\n- 1.0\n- Playful, expressive\n- Moderate risk of drift\n- High creativity\n- Brainstorming, entertainment agents\n{% /table %}\n\n## **Conclusion**\n\nLLM temperature shapes the heart and soul of voice AI interactions. It's the difference between an agent reading from a manual and one that feels like a trusted advisor. Need factual precision? Stay cool at 0.2-0.4. Want engaging sales conversations? You listen to what they say and remember their responses for context as the conversation evolves.\u0026nbsp;\n\nHuman conversations layer meaning, reference previous statements, and build toward solutions. Multi-turn capabilities let voice agents work in the same way.\n\n### **Single-Turn vs. Multiturn: The Critical Difference**\n\n**Single-turn interactions** work like this:\n\n- \"What are your hours?\" → Direct answer, conversation ends.\n- \"Set a timer for 10 minutes.\" → Command executed, done.\n- \"What's my account balance?\" → Number provided, next.\n\n**Multiturn conversations** unfold differently:\n\n- \"Can I change my flight?\" → \"Which reservation?\" → \"The one to Denver\" → \"What's the change fee?\" → \"That seems high, are there other options?\" →\n- \"I need help with my order.\" → \"What's the issue?\" → \"It hasn't arrived.\" → \"Let me check the tracking...\" → \"Can you reroute it to my office instead?\" →\n\nIt doesn’t take an expert in AI to understand the benefits of multi-turn voice capabilities. Single-turn has its value, but we expect your next voice agent build to be tailored to extended interactions. Multi-turn conversations are where the value increases dramatically.\u0026nbsp;\n\n**» [Speak to a multi-turn voice agent](https://vapi.ai/custom-agents/billing-inquiry-agent) designed for customer billing inquiries.**\n\n### **The Context Problem**\n\nMulti-turn sounds like an obvious solution to single interaction voice AI: obviously, more responses are better. Maintaining context across multiple exchanges requires sophisticated memory management, which most basic systems lack entirely.
